title: ⭐⭐ Practice: the habit that stopped, the aim behind the act

questions.prompt: A youth centre in El Kef prints a short note about a former member. Complete both gaps: "Wassim finished his two-year ___ in accountancy last June, and in September the bank gave him six weeks of ___ before he sat down at a desk of his own."

options.text: training / degree
scholarship / internship
degree / training
internship / scholarship

questions.explanation: "degree / training" fills the two gaps: a degree is the qualification the university hands you at the end of your studies, which is what two-year in accountancy describes, and training is the period during which somebody is taught to do the job itself, which is what the bank gives him in September. "training / degree" swaps them and produces two impossibilities: a university does not deliver a two-year training in accountancy in this sense, and a bank does not hand out degrees. "scholarship / internship" puts money where a qualification belongs, since a scholarship is a sum given to a student, and then calls internship a period spent inside the very company that already employs him, when an internship is served before you are hired. And "internship / scholarship" makes the second half say that the bank gave him six weeks of money for his studies, which he has already finished.

questions.prompt: Read this note a pupil wrote about her neighbour. "Aunt Zohra opened her own tailor's shop in Nabeul at twenty-four. For thirty years she sewed wedding dresses for the whole street. She sold the shop and the machines in 2021. She mends her grandchildren's clothes every week." The pupil wants to rewrite one of these four facts with "used to", and only one of them will take it. Which fact?

options.text: She sewed wedding dresses for the whole street.
She opened her own tailor's shop in Nabeul at twenty-four.
She mends her grandchildren's clothes every week.
She sold the shop and the machines in 2021.

questions.explanation: "She sewed wedding dresses for the whole street." is the one: it lasted thirty years, it was repeated week after week, and the shop has been sold, so the habit is over — which is exactly what used to says, and the note becomes She used to sew wedding dresses for the whole street. "She opened her own tailor's shop in Nabeul at twenty-four." happened once, on one day; a single event takes the past simple and never used to, whatever its date. "She sold the shop and the machines in 2021." is a single event as well, and it even carries its year, which closes the question. And "She mends her grandchildren's clothes every week." is a habit she still has today; used to would announce that she has stopped, and the note says the opposite.

questions.prompt: A school magazine in Gafsa is reporting on the book sale its club ran last month. The editor has four lines in front of her. Three of them say what came of the sale; one says what the club was aiming at when it fixed the price. Which line gives the aim?

options.text: The club sold the books at half price, so almost nothing was left by four o'clock.
The club sold the books at half price, and as a result the takings paid for the whole trip.
The club sold the books at half price; therefore the shelves were empty by the evening.
The club sold the books at half price so that the youngest pupils could afford them.

questions.explanation: "The club sold the books at half price so that the youngest pupils could afford them." gives the aim: so that opens a clause of purpose, it names the people the aim was for, and it says what the club wanted before it fixed the price — nothing in the line promises that it worked. "The club sold the books at half price, so almost nothing was left by four o'clock." uses so on its own, one word shorter and a whole meaning apart: so reports the result, what the reporter saw at four o'clock. "The club sold the books at half price, and as a result the takings paid for the whole trip." says as a result, which announces a consequence in the plainest terms possible. And "The club sold the books at half price; therefore the shelves were empty by the evening." points backwards at a cause that has already produced its effect; a purpose looks forward, a consequence looks back.

questions.prompt: Nizar had three weeks to send in his application for the summer course in Sousse. He put it off, filled the form in on the last evening and posted it the next morning; it reached the office two days after the closing date. He is talking about it to his sister now. Which sentence says what he thinks?

options.text: I should have left it until the last evening.
I shouldn't have left it until the last evening.
I shouldn't leave it until the last evening.
I didn't have to leave it until the last evening.

questions.explanation: "I shouldn't have left it until the last evening." is what he thinks: shouldn't have says that the thing was done and ought not to have been, which is exactly his case, and the past participle left puts the whole matter beyond repair. "I should have left it until the last evening." turns the facts round: should have says that the thing was not done, so the line would mean that he sent the form early and now regrets it. "I shouldn't leave it until the last evening." is advice for a form that has not been sent yet; the closing date has passed, and a present modal cannot reach a decision that is over. And "I didn't have to leave it until the last evening." only says that nothing obliged him to wait, which is true and beside the point: an absence of obligation is not a regret, and the sentence blames nobody, not even himself.

questions.prompt: Hichem has spent four months at the same counter, doing the same three tasks every morning, and this week he has started looking for something else. Complete the line he writes to a friend: "By the end of March I was fed up ___ the same three things every day."

options.text: of doing
to do
with doing
with to do

questions.explanation: "with doing" is the form: fed up takes the preposition with, and after a preposition an English verb goes into its -ing form, so the expression is always fed up with doing something. "of doing" chooses the wrong preposition, the one many learners hear in fed up of; the -ing form is right, the little word in front of it is not. "with to do" keeps the right preposition and then breaks the rule that follows it: after with, English never puts an infinitive. And "to do" drops the preposition altogether, which is what your own language would let you do; in English fed up is never followed directly by a verb.

questions.prompt: Emna's class has to hand in an interview, and her first question is for a retired nurse from El Kef. She wants to ask the woman whether night shifts were a regular part of her work in those years. Which question does she write?

options.text: Do you use to work at night?
Have you used to work at night?
Did you used to work at night?
Did you use to work at night?

questions.explanation: "Did you use to work at night?" is the question: the interrogative of used to is built with did, and did already carries the past, so the verb behind it loses its -d and comes back to use. "Did you used to work at night?" is the commonest mistake of all: it marks the past twice, once on did and once on used, and English marks it only once. "Do you use to work at night?" puts the question in the present, where it would ask about the nurse's working life today, and she has retired. And "Have you used to work at night?" borrows the auxiliary of the present perfect, which used to never takes; the two forms belong to opposite messages, since the present perfect ties the past to now and used to says that it is over.
